key_terms.meaning: Only the intended reader can understand the message; delivered by encryption.
The data has not been altered; delivered by hash functions and MACs.
Proof of who sent a message or who is asking for access.
The signer cannot later deny having signed; delivered by digital signatures.
One shared secret key does both encryption and decryption (AES is the common one).
A keyed hash, MAC = H(key ‖ message); detects tampering and forgery but not who signed.
H(x) squeezes any input to a fixed n-bit output and is one-way and collision-resistant.
Finding x ≠ y with H(x) = H(y) is practically impossible.
Given a hash h, finding any x with H(x) = h is infeasible.
Changing one input bit changes about half of the 256 output bits.
A pair (address of previous block, hash of its contents); the address finds the block, the hash checks it.
Binary tree where sibling hashes are combined pairwise until one root hash remains.
The single 32-byte hash in the block header that commits to every transaction in the block.
The log₂ n sibling hashes needed to recompute the root from one transaction hash.
A secret 256-bit number d used to sign; anyone holding it controls the money.
The curve point Q = d × G computed from the private key d; safe to publish.
Adding the generator point G to itself d times to get Q; easy forward, infeasible to reverse.
Adding a point P to itself on the curve: draw the tangent at P, reflect the second intersection to get 2P.
Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm; produces the pair (r, s) from a message hash and the private key.
Base58Check of version byte ‖ RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(public key)) ‖ 4-byte checksum.

takeaways: Cryptography supplies four separate tools — hashing, symmetric encryption, MACs and public-key operations — and each one answers a different security question.
A cryptographic hash is a one-way, collision-resistant fingerprint of fixed length; SHA-256 always outputs 256 bits = 32 bytes.
A hash pointer makes a block self-checking: change any old block and every later hash pointer fails, so tampering is visible from that point onward.
A Merkle tree lets a 32-byte root in the block header stand in for thousands of transactions, and a proof of membership costs only log₂ n hashes.
Public-key cryptography uses a trapdoor: multiplying the generator point by the private key is fast, dividing back is infeasible.
Elliptic curves give the same security as RSA with far shorter keys, which is why a 256-bit Bitcoin key is enough.
ECDSA proves the holder of a private key approved a specific message hash; the signature is (r, s) and is checked using only the public key.
A blockchain identity is just a key pair; the address is a shortened hash of the public key, not the key itself, which adds a layer of protection.
Reusing the ECDSA nonce k leaks the private key, so k must be fresh and unpredictable for every signature.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on precise definitions plus worked steps: state the property, show the formula, and trace tamper detection or signature verification block by block, with numbers.

bank.q: Explain the four security goals of cryptography — confidentiality, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation — and name the cryptographic tool that delivers each one.
outline: Define each goal in one line
Confidentiality → symmetric or public-key encryption
Integrity → hash function, MAC, digital signature
Authentication → MAC with shared key, or signature with private key
Non-repudiation → digital signature only, because a shared key can be denied by either party
Give one blockchain use of each

bank.q: List the properties a cryptographic hash function must satisfy and describe how SHA-256 processes a message to produce a 256-bit digest.
outline: Preimage resistance, second-preimage resistance, collision resistance, avalanche effect
Fixed output length 256 bits = 32 bytes regardless of input size
Padding to a multiple of 512 bits with the length appended
Message schedule and 64 rounds over eight 32-bit working variables
Final addition of the initial hash values gives the digest
State why collision resistance matters for proof of work

bank.q: What is a hash pointer? Explain how hash pointers link blocks into a chain and how they make the chain tamper-evident.
outline: Definition: address of previous block + hash of its contents
Difference from an ordinary pointer
Block header field prev_block hash
Editing block i changes its hash, so the pointer in block i+1 no longer matches
All later blocks must be re-mined; state the work involved
Genesis block has no previous pointer

bank.q: Describe the construction of a Merkle tree for n transactions and explain how a Merkle proof is verified using the block header.
outline: Leaf = H(transaction), pairs combined as H(left ‖ right)
Odd node is duplicated or promoted upward
Levels halve each step until one root remains
Root stored in the 80-byte block header
Proof = sibling hashes along the path, log₂ n of them
Verifier recomputes upward and compares with the header root
Use for SPV clients that do not download full blocks

bank.q: Explain public-key cryptography using elliptic curves: key generation, the role of the generator point, and why the private key cannot be computed from the public key.
outline: Private key d = random integer in [1, n−1]
Public key Q = d × G, G is the standard generator on secp256k1
Curve equation y² = x³ + 7 (mod p) with stated p and n
Point addition and point doubling rules, geometric meaning
Scalar multiplication by double-and-add
Discrete log problem: given Q and G, finding d is infeasible
Key sizes: 256-bit ECC roughly equals 3072-bit RSA

bank.q: A block contains 4096 transactions. How many hashes does a Merkle proof for one transaction contain, and how many hashes would a node need without a Merkle tree? Show the working.
outline: 4096 = 2¹², so tree height is 12
Proof = 12 × 32 bytes = 384 bytes
Without a tree the verifier needs all 4096 hashes = 131 072 bytes
Compare the two and state the saving ratio
Mention that the root is still 32 bytes in the header

bank.q: Starting from a 256-bit private key, list the steps to derive a Bitcoin address and give the approximate length of the final address.
outline: Private key d → public key Q = d × G (33-byte compressed or 65-byte uncompressed)
SHA-256 of the public key
RIPEMD-160 of that result gives the 20-byte hash160
Prepend version byte (0x00 for mainnet)
Double SHA-256, take the first 4 bytes as checksum
Append checksum and encode in Base58
Result is about 26–35 characters beginning with 1

bank.q: A transaction hash is the third leaf in an 8-leaf Merkle tree. Given the three sibling hashes supplied in the proof, show step by step how a light client checks that this transaction is in the block.
outline: Concatenate leaf with its sibling in the correct left/right order
Hash to get the parent
Repeat with the next sibling at the next level
After three rounds one hash remains
Compare it byte for byte with merkle_root in the header
Equal → membership proven; different → reject
Note what happens if the order left/right is swapped

bank.q: Describe how a sender signs a transaction hash with ECDSA and how a node verifies the signature using the public key. Include the roles of r, s, k and the message hash z.
outline: Choose random nonce k, compute point R = k × G, set r = R.x mod n
s = k⁻¹(z + r·d) mod n
Signature is (r, s), published with the transaction
Verifier computes w = s⁻¹ mod n, u₁ = z·w, u₂ = r·w
Point P = u₁·G + u₂·Q; check P.x mod n equals r
Any change to the message changes z and the check fails
Note: k must never repeat — reuse leaks d

bank.q: Compare a simple hash chain of blocks with a Merkle-tree block structure for tamper detection and for light-client verification. Which is better and why?
outline: Hash chain detects any edit with a single hash comparison per block
Merkle tree adds per-transaction membership proofs of size log₂ n
A full block download is O(n); a Merkle proof is O(log n)
Header alone (80 bytes) plus proof lets an SPV client verify a payment
Hash chain alone gives no per-transaction proof without the whole block
Conclusion: hash pointers give chain integrity, Merkle trees give scalable inclusion proofs
Mention the cost: tree construction and storage of intermediate hashes

bank.q: An attacker modifies one transaction inside block 100 of a chain whose latest block is 106. Trace what breaks and evaluate how deep the attack must go to succeed.
outline: Transaction hash changes → Merkle root changes
Block 100 header hash changes
prev_block hash inside block 101 no longer matches
Every block from 101 to 106 must be recomputed
New proof of work needed for each of those blocks
Attacker must out-mine the honest network, and other nodes reject the longest-chain rule if outrun
Conclusion: cost grows with confirmation depth; six confirmations is a common practice

bank.q: Bitcoin addresses are 20-byte hashes of the public key rather than the public key itself. Evaluate the security and size reasons for this choice.
outline: Size: 20 bytes vs 33/65 bytes in every output, saves block space
Extra hash layer means the public key is not revealed until spending
Attackers must break hash preimage and elliptic-curve discrete log
Hash160 also shortens and standardises identity
Risk: sending to a mistyped address, mitigated by Base58Check checksum
No identity is embedded — an address is pseudonymous, not anonymous

bank.q: Explain why ECDSA fails completely if the same nonce k is used for two different messages, and derive the private key in that case.
outline: Two signatures share r because r = (k × G).x mod n
s₁ = k⁻¹(z₁ + r·d), s₂ = k⁻¹(z₂ + r·d) mod n
Subtract: s₁ − s₂ = k⁻¹(z₁ − z₂) mod n
So k = (z₁ − z₂)(s₁ − s₂)⁻¹ mod n
Then d = (s₁·k − z₁)·r⁻¹ mod n
Conclude: the private key is exposed publicly and funds are lost
Rule: k must be random or derived deterministically (RFC 6979)

bank.q: Distinguish between symmetric encryption, message authentication codes, hash functions and digital signatures. Which of these does a blockchain use, and for what?
outline: Shared-key vs two-key tools in a table
Hash function: no key, integrity only, used for block linking and PoW
MAC: shared key, integrity plus authentication between two parties
Digital signature: private key signs, anyone verifies, gives non-repudiation, used for transactions
Symmetric encryption is rarely used on-chain; keys and wallets may encrypt locally
State that a MAC cannot settle a dispute because both parties hold the key

glossary.def: The science of writing messages so that only the intended reader can read or verify them.
The original readable message before any cryptographic operation.
The unreadable output produced after encrypting plaintext.
A secret or public value that controls an encryption, hash-based or signature operation.
A function that maps an input of any size to an output of fixed size.
The fixed-size output of a hash function, also called the hash value.
The SHA-2 member that always produces a 256-bit (32-byte) digest; used twice in Bitcoin's block hashing.
Two different inputs x and y that produce the same hash H(x) = H(y).
A search that finds a hash collision in about 2^(n/2) tries instead of 2^n.
A small change in input causing a large, unpredictable change in output bits.
The 80-byte summary of a block holding version, previous block hash, Merkle root, time, bits and nonce.
The first block of a chain, which has no previous block pointer.
A pointer that gives both the location of some data and the hash of that data, so the data can be checked.
A structure in which any change is detectable, even if the change cannot be prevented.
A binary tree of hashes that reduces many data items to a single root hash.
A light-client method that checks a transaction using block headers and Merkle proofs instead of full blocks.
A scheme with a public key for verifying or encrypting and a private key for signing or decrypting.
A curve of the form y² = x³ + ax + b over a finite field, on which a group of points is defined.
The specific elliptic curve Bitcoin uses, with equation y² = x³ + 7 over a 256-bit prime field.
The fixed base point on the curve from which every public key is computed as d × G.
The hard problem of recovering d from Q = d × G on an elliptic curve.
A value attached to a message that proves the signer holds the private key and that the message is unchanged.
The one-time random number used inside ECDSA; it must never repeat for two different messages.
An encoding that uses 58 safe characters and appends a 4-byte double-SHA-256 checksum so typos are caught.
A short derived value stored with data so that accidental errors can be detected on read.
A Base58Check encoding of a single private key, used to move keys between wallets.
